overview: Ancient Armenia was a succession of highland kingdoms, not one unchanging dynasty. These two map records cover 323 to 200 BCE and 1 BCE to 400 CE; the gap is an atlas omission, not a disappearance of Armenia. Orontid, Artaxiad and Arsacid rulers connected the country with Iranian and Mediterranean worlds.

periods.title: Orontid Armenia
periods.summary: After Alexander, Orontid rulers maintained kingdoms in the Armenian highlands.

periods.title: Artaxiad monarchy and empire
periods.summary: Artaxias founded a new dynasty in 189 BCE. Its greatest expansion came under Tigranes II; the line ended around 12 CE.

periods.title: A contested throne
periods.summary: Roman and Parthian candidates competed until a compromise recognized Tiridates I, crowned at Rome in 66.

periods.title: Arsacid rule
periods.summary: Arsacid kings governed among powerful hereditary princes while negotiating with rival empires.

periods.title: Christianization and partition
periods.summary: Christianity gained royal support early in the fourth century. Partition around 387 divided Armenia between Roman and Iranian spheres.

sections.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire

items.text: The Orontids linked Armenian kingship to the earlier Iranian imperial world while operating among Hellenistic powers. Their history survives unevenly in Greek authors, inscriptions and coins. A dynasty could adopt new diplomatic partners without replacing every local institution or family.

Artaxias I set up inscribed boundary stones on the lands of towns and estates. Such markers made royal authority visible where a dispute could be painfully practical: whose field, and whose harvest? Archaeologists have recovered multiple stones bearing Aramaic inscriptions.

Tigranes II, ruling approximately 95 to 55 BCE, expanded Armenia into a major power between Rome and Parthia. His conquests included Sophene and Syria. The imperial maximum belongs between the two imported map intervals, so neither outline should be treated as a picture of his whole empire.

Conquest did not guarantee a permanent empire. After wars against Roman commanders, Tigranes reached a settlement with Pompey in 66 BCE. He lost his wider conquests but retained the Armenian kingdom and continued to rule. Losing an empire was not the same event as the disappearance of Armenia.

Arsacid government involved bargaining with hereditary princely houses. Kings tried to strengthen their own authority; powerful nobles defended inherited positions and possessions. Palace politics therefore depended on regional families as well as on relations with Rome and Iran.

Artaxata became an Armenian royal capital in the second century BCE. Its buildings used earth as well as stone. Researchers examined mudbrick with microscopes and material analyses, turning apparently ordinary lumps of soil into evidence for how builders organized their work.

The mudbrick study suggests that Hellenistic builders remade material from older Urartian bricks. Old earth could be broken down, mixed with water and fresh temper, and shaped again. Recycling here meant manufacturing new bricks from old material: a much older idea than the modern recycling bin.

Pottery from Artaxata’s Hill XIII records a change in how buildings were used. Early complexes, dating to the second and first centuries BCE, contained many fine vessels and may have served public or sanctuary functions. Later domestic occupation brought more cooking pots and storage jars.

A study of 53 ceramic samples found that most of the examined pottery was made locally. Fine tableware, coarse vessels and turquoise-glazed wares involved different recipes or workshops. A household’s dishes could therefore connect it with several specialized producers within the same city.

Cooking and storage vessels give archaeologists a route into household work that royal histories often ignore. At Artaxata, the increased number of such pots is evidence for domestic activity; the shapes alone do not supply a complete dinner menu or tell us exactly who cooked.

Excavations in 1979 and 1980 recovered roughly 8,000 seal impressions on Artaxata’s Hill V, with a much smaller group on Hill VIII. These small clay marks outlasted the documents they once helped secure. For archaeologists, administrative paperwork can survive as its packaging.

Were those seals from private business or a public archive? A modern reassessment compares their size, imagery and administrative character and argues for a city archive. The interpretation remains an archaeological argument, but it makes the collection important evidence for organized record keeping.

An aqueduct discovered outside Artaxata was a water project that never reached completion. Excavators connect its foundations with Trajan’s Roman occupation, approximately 114 to 117 CE. After Trajan died, Hadrian relinquished the province and construction stopped. These pillars are evidence of an interrupted plan, not proof of running taps.

The aqueduct first appeared to investigators as a dotted line in a magnetic survey. Excavation, drilling, drone imagery and mortar analysis helped explain the pattern. The broad scientific dating was less precise than the historical attribution: archaeology combines several clues rather than producing a date stamped on every stone.

At Artaxata, a church announced in 2024 has an octagonal plan with cross-shaped extensions. Surviving wooden platforms were radiocarbon-dated to the middle of the fourth century. The building provides physical evidence for an early Christian community, alongside the written traditions about Armenia’s conversion.

The church measured about 30 metres across and had mortar flooring, terracotta tiles and fragments of imported Mediterranean marble. Its builders and patrons invested in a substantial shared religious space. The excavators had not yet established its dedication: finding a church does not automatically reveal its name.

sections.title: Families, coins and words that survive

items.text: A copper coin from Artaxata names Queen Erato alongside a King Tigranes. Oxford’s catalogue leaves the attribution uncertain between Tigranes III and V, with possible dates around 10 or 5 BCE or 6 CE. A royal woman is visible here through money, even when the exact reign remains debated.

The coin’s Greek reverse reads Ἐρατὼ βασιλέως Τιγράνου ἀδελφή, transliterated Eratō basileōs Tigranou adelphē: “Erato, sister of King Tigranes.” This is a catalogue transcription of an ancient coin legend, not Armenian script. It shows how a royal family relationship could become a public message.

An earlier writing sample comes from Artaxias’s boundary stones: MLK RWNDKN, translated by the scholar James Russell as “Orontid king.” This is scholarly transliteration of Aramaic, with an alternative reading noted in the publication. Artaxias advertised inherited legitimacy even while establishing a new dynasty.

Armenian is an Indo-European language with extensive Iranian influence, but it is not simply a form of Persian. Its own alphabet was created by Mesrop Mashtots around 405, just after these map records end. Surviving Armenian literary writing therefore belongs to a later phase than the Aramaic and Greek witnesses shown here.

ending.text: Neither 200 BCE nor 400 CE marks Armenia’s disappearance. After partition around 387, an eastern Armenian monarchy survived until its abolition in 428 under Sasanian authority. Armenian communities, aristocratic families and the church continued through the political change.
